newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Major says no bargaining over IRA truce.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Major says no bargaining over IRA truce.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major said on Thursday he was not prepared to change British government policy and bargain with the Irish Republican Army or its political wing Sinn Fein over a new ceasefire in Northern Ireland.
Major told parliament the government was not trying to erect new hurdles in the path of the peace process.
But he said there was no chance of Sinn Fein joining multi-party peace talks until IRA guerrillas fighting to unite Ireland reinstated a ceasefire, broken in February.

"When Sinn Fein can join the talks depends upon their own actions. We need to see an unequivocal restoration of the ceasefire. We need to be able to make a credible judgment that it's lasting...We are not seeking delay," Major told parliament.
"We wish to see inclusive talks involving all parties as soon as possible but if Sinn Fein continue to exclude themselves, the talks must and will go on without them."
"We cannot and we will not change our policy to bargain for a ceasefire," he said.

Major was answering a question in parliament after talks between the government and John Hume, the leader of the Catholic nationalist SDLP party, who has been trying to break the deadlock over Sinn Fein's participation in peace talks.

In a statement issued as Major was speaking, the government said Hume had suggested a new IRA ceasefire, which the nationalist politician believed would become permanent, was available if Britain clarified its position on various issues.
These included the length of the multi-party peace talks, the scrapping of guerrilla arms, known as decommissioning, and ways of building confidence in the British-ruled province.
But the statement said Major had consistently made clear the government would welcome a new IRA ceasefire but was sceptical about how credible it would be.
The IRA abandoned a 17-month ceasefire in February with a series of bombings on the British mainland.

But the guerrillas have not carried out any attacks for nearly two months since an attack on an army base in Northern Ireland killed one soldier, raising speculation that they are operating an unofficial truce to win concessions for Sinn Fein.
Major told parliament: "There has been a great deal of rumour and disinformation in recent weeks."
"We have made it absolutely clear throughout those exchanges that the IRA and Sinn Fein should give up violence and commit themselves to exclusively peaceful means."
Irish prime minister John Bruton on Thursday called for patience as both Catholics and Protestants clamoured for a public response from Britain to the republican ceasefire plan.
Bruton is to meet Major in London on December 9 to discuss Northern Ireland and Hume's efforts.

Irish leaders have sought to smooth over London's coolness over the Hume proposals, saying talks to try to get a new IRA ceasefire and to bring republican leaders into talks on the future of the province were still underway.
But pro-British "Loyalists" had called on Major to publish his response to the Hume proposals, saying they suspected Britain had been doing secret deals with the republicans.
The statement issued on Thursday included Major's response to Hume and the way the British government envisaged taking the peace process forward if the IRA announced a ceasefire.

The government said this would include meetings with Sinn Fein to explore what assurances they could give and to give the IRA's political wing the change to make a total and absolute commitment to democratic, non-violent principles.
There would then be meetings with all political parties to see how to take the process forward. One this was concluded, Sinn Fein would be invited into all-party talks.

Some decommissioning would have to take place during all-party negotiations, the statement said, "so that the process of decommissioning is not seen as a block to progress...but can be used to build confidence one step at a time".
